title: Guarding the zero case
idea: A guard is a simple if that handles the edge case first, so the normal code only runs when it is safe. Read guards and predict them.

options: an if that handles the edge case before the normal code
exercises.explanation: A guard is an if that checks for the dangerous or empty case first, keeping the normal path safe.
count is 0, so the guard's condition is True: it prints No items and skips the normal branch.
count is 4, so count == 0 is False; the else (normal case) runs: We have items.

exercises.prompt: A guard lets the normal code run only when the edge case did NOT happen.
exercises.explanation: Right. The guard catches the edge case; the else (or the code after) handles the safe, normal case.

exercises.prompt: Which condition guards against dividing by zero in total / count?
exercises.explanation: You guard the divisor: check if count == 0 first, so you only divide when count is not zero.

exercises.prompt: Order a safe plan for 'average = total / count'.
blocks: If zero, say there is no average
exercises.explanation: Guard the zero first, then divide only in the safe case. The edge case never reaches the division.
people is 0, so the guard fires: No one to share with. The division in the else is safely skipped.
Use == to test if count equals 0. The guard then catches the empty case.

exercises.prompt: Why put the guard FIRST, before the division?
options: So the unsafe division never runs when count is zero
exercises.explanation: Checking the edge case first means the risky code only runs when it is safe. Order protects the program.

options: an if/else used to handle the edge case
exercises.explanation: A guard is the same if/else you already know, aimed at the edge case. No new syntax - just a smart use of it.
